sections.heading: SPEA, the permit and the questions worth asking locally
paragraphs: Al Qasimia has a mature tutoring market, which is a mixed blessing: plenty of choice, and plenty of arrangements made on a neighbour's recommendation with no questions asked. Two questions are worth asking, and both are cheap.

The first is the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those operating without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule is published, so disregard any figure quoted at you. Because the permit is free, a working tutor has no reason not to hold one.

The second question concerns conflicts. Do not arrange tuition with your child's own class teacher. Abu Dhabi's regulator has published professional-ethics rules barring school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct pointing the same way. The arrangement feels convenient and creates a conflict of interest in marking and reporting that nobody benefits from.

On the school side, private education in Sharjah is regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which regulates private schools in the emirate and, along with Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge, approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses and assessment methods. So your school's assessment calendar is documented, and asking for it in writing is an ordinary request. For our own position: IB Gram holds no approval, licence or accreditation from SPEA or any other UAE authority, and we have no premises in this country.

sections.heading: Assessed work, deadlines and the line we do not cross
paragraphs: Pressure in a collision fortnight is exactly when the boundary around assessed work gets tested, which is why it should be agreed in calm weather. The permitted zone is wide enough that a well-supported student never needs to go near the edge.

A tutor may read the criteria with the student, question a research question until it is answerable with available data, teach a technique or a statistical method the work requires, review a draft and explain which criterion it fails, and model the same analytical move on different material. A tutor may not write, draft, rewrite or edit any part of the submitted work, and may not provide a topic with the analysis already done.

IB Gram does not sell completed internal assessments, extended essays, Theory of Knowledge essays or coursework. Services that do appear in these search results at prices in the thousands of dirhams. The consequence of using one is a malpractice finding against the student's diploma, which no deadline justifies and no tutoring fee offsets.

The genuine defence is the calendar, which is where this page started. Students who read the criteria in week one, agree an internal deadline earlier than the school's, and show a draft to somebody three weeks out are not the students negotiating with an essay mill at midnight. That sequence costs a few short sessions and is most of what our coursework coaching actually consists of.

One related point about materials. Syllabus documents, past papers and mark schemes belong to the boards, so we cite the official sources and point families to the school for current versions rather than distributing copies. A service offering a shared drive of 'exclusive' board material is handing out somebody else's copyright, and where the material is unreleased it creates a malpractice question attached to your child rather than to the seller.

process.title: Tell us the week, not just the subject
process.description: Send the subject and level, the school finish time, the commute, and any fixed commitments - mandatory subject homework, sport, a sibling's slot. We place the hour where it can actually survive a term rather than where it looks neat on a calendar.

process.title: Ask the school for its deadline list
process.description: We will ask you for the internal deadline calendar: internal assessment submission dates, extended essay checkpoints, the Theory of Knowledge deadline, mock windows. Most schools supply it on request. With that list the collision fortnight becomes visible months in advance.

process.title: Free trial lesson, then a fixed slot
process.description: The trial is one-to-one over live video at no cost, and it tests the slot as much as the tutor. If the time does not work in practice, we move it before the term starts rather than letting attendance decay in week three.

process.title: Review at six sessions, and change the shape if needed
process.description: We look at timed scores and criterion feedback rather than attendance. Sometimes the right answer is a different tutor; sometimes it is a shorter, more frequent pattern, or a weekend morning instead of a weekday evening. We would rather change the shape than extend a plan that is not working.

whyPoints.title: The slot is protected, not aspirational
whyPoints.description: Lessons start when the student is at the desk. A late school bus moves the session by twenty minutes instead of cancelling it, because nobody is driving anywhere. In central Sharjah that single property is the difference between twelve sessions a term and eight.

whyPoints.title: The hour changes with the term
whyPoints.description: Content in DP1, proposals in the third term, assessed work in DP2's first half, timed papers in the final term. We revisit the plan every few weeks instead of spending the same hour the same way all year.

whyPoints.title: The collision fortnight is planned for
whyPoints.description: We ask for the school's internal deadline calendar at the start of DP2 so the fortnight where everything lands is visible in advance. When it arrives, we switch to short frequent check-ins rather than adding teaching the student has no capacity to absorb.

whyPoints.title: Delivery described accurately
whyPoints.description: All UAE lessons are one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not run home visits in the UAE; that service exists only in India. Nobody books expecting a car and receives a video call.

whyPoints.title: Assessed work stays the student's
whyPoints.description: Criteria, questions, method and feedback - yes. Writing or editing the submitted text - never, and we do not sell completed assessments. The malpractice risk falls on the student, so the boundary is not a matter of preference.

faqs.question: Will an IB tutor come to an apartment in Al Qasimia?
faqs.answer: Tutors in the central Sharjah market do visit homes, at rates quoted between roughly AED 180 and 500 an hour once travel is absorbed. IB Gram does not: we run no home visits anywhere in the UAE, because that service exists only in India. For a family here the practical gain is reliability - a lesson delivered over live video starts when your child sits down, shifts by twenty minutes when the bus is late, and never disappears because of traffic on Al Wahda Street. The free trial lesson lets you test the format at no cost.

faqs.question: What time of day actually works for IB tutoring in central Sharjah?
faqs.answer: For most families, five-thirty to seven-thirty on two or three weekdays, and mid-morning at the weekend. Earlier than five works only with a short school run; after eight produces attendance rather than learning. The weekend morning is the most underused hour in the week - nobody is tired, nothing else is scheduled, and ninety minutes of internal assessment work is genuinely possible. Households with children at several schools usually do best placing slots back to back on one evening so a parent supervises once rather than three times.

faqs.question: How do the mandatory UAE subjects affect an IB student's evening?
faqs.answer: They fill the day. Private schools must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum under federal regulations, and instructional time for those subjects is counted in forty-minute lesson units. So a Diploma student arrives home with homework from six subjects plus work from the mandatory lessons. The practical consequence is that a long general session competes with homework and loses; a short specific one on the next dated piece of work survives. We keep sessions to the hour and end them on time.

faqs.question: Which IB deadlines should I ask my child's school for in writing?
faqs.answer: At the start of DP2, ask the coordinator for internal assessment submission dates per subject, the extended essay checkpoints, the Theory of Knowledge essay deadline and the mock windows. These internal dates bind your child and sit earlier than anything the board publishes. Most schools provide the list on request and very few families ask. We do not publish IB examination or results dates here because we could not verify them from the IB's own site; the coordinator holds the confirmed version for your school.

faqs.question: What is the collision fortnight in DP2 and can it be avoided?
faqs.answer: It is the predictable window where two internal assessments, a Theory of Knowledge draft, a set of tests and revision all arrive together. It cannot be avoided but it can be defused by finishing one piece early, which requires knowing the dates months ahead. When the window arrives, the useful support is sequencing rather than teaching: deciding what gets finished first, what an acceptable standard is for each piece, and what waits. Three short check-ins in that fortnight beat two long lessons, and we switch pattern deliberately.

faqs.question: Is the summer between DP1 and DP2 worth booking sessions in?
faqs.answer: It is the most efficient window in the programme. Nothing is due, no tests compete, and three or four sessions can settle an exploration question, plan an investigation's method or clear a content backlog that would otherwise surface during revision. Families in Al Qasimia often travel for part of the break; because lessons are delivered over live video, the slot follows the student with a timezone adjustment. Students who use the summer start DP2 level; students who do not spend the first month catching up while deadlines begin.

faqs.question: How does Ramadan change a weekly IB slot?
faqs.answer: It moves it. School days shorten, afternoons are low-energy, and the productive hours become late morning at the weekend and after Iftar. The important thing is to rewrite the plan before the month begins rather than improvising through it, particularly for a DP2 student with an assessed deadline inside the window. Because the lesson is online, moving a slot by two hours costs nothing and requires no renegotiation of anybody's journey. Eid then removes several days, so build slack into deadlines ahead of the break.

faqs.question: What does a term of IB tutoring cost in Sharjah?
faqs.answer: A term is about twelve teaching weeks, so a weekly slot is twelve hours. At market rates - a qualified subject tutor teaching online runs roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour across published UAE rate cards - that is in the region of AED 1,800 to 3,600 per subject per term. The in-home equivalent for the same hours sits higher, with travel priced in. Bestimate's Dubai estimates, read in October 2026, put a weekly session at AED 600 to 1,200 a month with a qualified tutor. Those are market figures, not our price list.

faqs.question: My child is in the Middle Years and the report mentions criteria. What should I look at?
faqs.answer: The criterion letters rather than the overall grade. Middle Years tasks are marked once against task-specific descriptors, so a weak task is outscored later rather than revised away, and a diligent student can score respectably while remaining weak on the criterion that asks for evaluation or justified conclusions. Read the descriptors with your child before the next task. Three or four sessions aimed at one criterion often lift the achievement level, and the skill transfers to every later task in that subject.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help during study leave when school teaching has stopped?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is one of the highest-value periods to use support. Once study leave begins, the structure a student has relied on for years disappears overnight, and unstructured days produce very little for most teenagers. A short daily or alternate-day check-in - twenty to thirty minutes, with a specific task set and reviewed - usually does more than a single weekly lesson. It also gives a parent visibility without turning every breakfast into an interrogation about revision.

faqs.question: Does a tutor in Sharjah need a MoHRE permit, and what should I ask?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tutor work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Ask whether they hold it; since it costs nothing, there is no good reason not to. Those tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine figure is published.

faqs.question: Is it a problem to hire my child's own subject teacher privately?
faqs.answer: It is a conflict you should avoid. Abu Dhabi's regulator has published professional-ethics rules prohibiting private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct points the same way. Beyond the rules, the arrangement puts the person who marks your child's work on your payroll, which compromises both the marking and the reporting. A specialist with no connection to the school gives you independent information about where your child actually stands.

faqs.question: How many of my child's six Diploma subjects should we support?
faqs.answer: Usually one or two. Look for the subject where the grade is genuinely blocking a university route, or where the internal assessment is at risk, and support that properly rather than spreading four thin slots across the week. A Diploma student has limited evening capacity, and adding four tutoring hours to an already full timetable tends to reduce independent study rather than increase learning. We will say when we think a family is buying more hours than the evidence supports.

faqs.question: What happens if our usual slot stops working mid-term?
faqs.answer: We move it, and we would rather move it than watch attendance decay. School commitments change, a sport season starts, a commute lengthens, and a slot that worked in September stops working in January. Because nobody is driving to an address, rescheduling is a matter of finding another hour with the same tutor, often within the same week. If the tutor's own availability no longer fits, we will match a different specialist and carry the written plan across rather than starting again.

sharjah/ib-home-tutor-in-al-qasimia.closingBody: Send three things: the subject and level, the school finish time and commute, and the fixed commitments the week already contains. If you have the school's internal deadline list, send that too. We will propose a slot that can survive a Sharjah term, match a specialist who has taught the course, and run a free trial lesson over live video at no cost. Lessons for Al Qasimia families are one-to-one and online, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, and they start when your child sits down rather than when somebody's car arrives.

intro.heading: The school run decides the tutoring, not the other way round
paragraphs: Al Rahmaniya is a low-density villa community on the western edge of Sharjah, close to Emirates Road and within reach of school clusters in three directions. Its families did not move here for the schools inside it; they move here for the housing and then drive or bus their children somewhere else. That single fact shapes everything about tutoring in this community.

Start with the arithmetic nobody writes down. A school day that ends at half past two does not put a child at a desk at three. There is the walk to the bus, the loading, the route around other communities, and the last ten minutes of a journey that is slower than it should be. For a school in Muwaileh or central Sharjah, arrival home between a quarter past three and four is normal. For a school across the Dubai boundary, between four and half past five.

Then there is what happens after arrival. A teenager who has been in uniform since half past six needs to eat and decompress. Homework from six Diploma subjects is waiting, along with work from the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies lessons that every private school in this country must timetable. The window for tutoring is real but narrow, and it sits later in the evening than most families plan for.

Now add a tutor who drives to Al Rahmaniya. Their journey happens in the same traffic as the school bus, from wherever they live, usually central Sharjah or Dubai. A session nominally at five o'clock starts at twenty past, finishes early because the next family is waiting, and gets cancelled outright on the two or three evenings a term when something goes wrong on Emirates Road. Families treat that as the price of living out here. It is not; it is a design flaw with an obvious fix.

Our arrangement removes the tutor's journey entirely. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, and they start when your child sits down. If the bus is twenty minutes late the lesson moves twenty minutes. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE - that service exists only in India - so there is no car to wait for and no travel premium inside the rate.

None of this is an argument that in-home tutoring is bad. It solves supervision, which is the real problem for some younger children, and a family in that position may well decide the premium is worth paying. It is simply not what we sell here, and the honest thing is to say so on the page rather than after a deposit.

The rest of this page works through the detail: which school clusters this community feeds and what each journey does to the evening, how to place a slot by bus time rather than bell time, how a longer IB commute changes the plan, what to do when siblings attend different schools, and what the school run costs a family in hours before anybody has paid for a lesson.

sections.heading: Which schools this community actually feeds
paragraphs: Al Rahmaniya has very little school provision inside it, so every family here is a commuting family. The directions they commute in fall into three groups, and each produces a different evening.

The nearest group is Muwaileh and University City, reached in fifteen to twenty-five minutes by car and rather longer by bus, because a bus collects from several communities. Children at these schools are generally home between a quarter past three and four, which is the most workable arrival time in the community.

The second group is central Sharjah: Al Majaz, Al Qasimia, Al Khan and the schools around them. The distance is not large but the afternoon traffic is, and buses from these schools serve a long route west. Arrival between four and half past is typical, which pushes a sensible session start to five or later.

The third group is Dubai, across the boundary. Al Rahmaniya sits close enough to Emirates Road that a Dubai school is a realistic choice, and plenty of families make it. The return journey is the longest in the household - frequently an hour or more - and a student can be home anywhere between four and half past five depending on the route and the day. For these families, a four o'clock tutoring slot is a fiction, and the weekend morning becomes genuinely valuable.
Working out which group your child is in takes one week of noticing the time they walk in. That number, rather than the school's published finish time, is the input a tutoring plan needs.

sections.heading: The gap between the bell and the desk
paragraphs: Schools publish a finish time and families plan around it, which is the root of a surprising amount of wasted tutoring money. The bell is the start of a process, not the end of the day.

Count the stages. Dismissal takes a few minutes. Walking to the bus and loading takes longer with younger children. The route home serves other communities first. Traffic on the roads out to the western communities is heaviest exactly then. For a secondary student with a cross-boundary school, the gap between bell and front door can be ninety minutes, and nothing about it is unusual.

After the front door, there is a second gap that matters just as much. A child who has been in uniform since dawn needs food and twenty minutes of nothing. Pushing a student into a session five minutes after arrival produces attendance rather than learning, and the tutor spends the first fifteen minutes managing mood instead of teaching. Thirty minutes of buffer is not indulgence; it is what makes the hour productive.

So the correct instruction is: take the real arrival time, add half an hour, and place the session there. If that lands at six, the session is at six. If it lands too late to be useful on a weekday, the honest conclusion is that this child should have one shorter weekday session and a longer weekend morning, rather than two weekday sessions that both underperform.

Parents can test this in a week without any effort. Note the time your child actually walks in on five consecutive days and take the latest of the five, not the average, because a plan built on the best day collapses on the worst one. The resulting number is usually forty minutes later than the one the family had in mind.

sections.heading: Why a tutor's own journey breaks the arrangement
paragraphs: Every problem described above applies to a tutor driving to Al Rahmaniya, with one difference: the tutor is doing it after their own working day, from wherever they live, to a community that is not on the way to anything.

The consequences are predictable. Start times drift. A session that drifts twenty minutes gets trimmed at the end because the tutor has another family waiting, so the family pays for sixty minutes and receives forty. On the evenings when Emirates Road is genuinely bad, the session is cancelled - usually at short notice, and usually in the term when it matters.

There is a quieter cost too. A tutor who has to travel to outlying communities limits how many of them they take, which means the pool of people willing to come here is smaller than the pool in central Sharjah. That pool is already generalist-weighted, and the subset who have taught a specific Diploma subject at a specific level is very small indeed. So the family that insists on an in-home visit is choosing from a short list of a short list.

Removing the journey removes all of that at once. The lesson starts when the student is ready, runs its full length, cannot be cancelled by traffic, and can be delivered by a specialist who lives anywhere in the country. We should be clear that in-home tutoring solves a real problem for some families, particularly supervision of younger children. It is simply not what IB Gram sells in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India.

sections.heading: The longer IB commute, and what it changes
paragraphs: Diploma provision in Sharjah sits in a small number of schools. That is a straightforward supply fact and it has two direct consequences for a family in Al Rahmaniya with an IB student.

The first is the commute. An IB child frequently has the longest journey in the household, either across the emirate or into Dubai. Their arrival time therefore sets the household's late slot, and their weekday capacity is lower than a sibling's at a nearer school. Expecting the same evening workload from both children is the most common planning error in these households.

The second is the tutoring pool. The number of adults in this emirate who have taught a specific Diploma subject to final grade standard is small, and the number of those willing to drive to a western villa community on a weekday evening is smaller again. For higher level sciences and the less common languages, the practical answer locally is often nobody. Over video, the same request is routine.

There is a knock-on effect on subject choice worth mentioning. Students who are already spending two hours a day travelling sometimes drop a higher level subject they could have managed, simply because the week has no room in it. A session placed properly, with the heavy work moved to the weekend, occasionally changes that calculation - which is a bigger return than a few marks.

What this means in practice is that an Al Rahmaniya IB student should be matched nationally and scheduled around their own arrival, with the heavier work - internal assessment planning, long past papers, extended essay checkpoints - moved to weekend mornings when concentration is available. That is a different plan from the one a Year 9 sibling at a Muwaileh school needs, and writing both down separately is what stops the household running on improvisation.

sections.heading: Siblings at different schools, on one evening
paragraphs: Households in this community commonly have children at two or even three schools, chosen at different times for different reasons. The result is a staggered set of arrival times and a parent on duty from four o'clock until bedtime.

Sequencing fixes most of it. Place the earliest arrival first - usually the primary child, who also needs the shortest session - then the middle child, then the student with the longest commute. Each gets their own specialist and their own plan, and the parent supervises a single evening instead of patrolling four.

The trick that makes this work is that nobody is driving. With in-home tutoring, consecutive slots mean either one tutor covering two very different courses, which usually shortchanges the older child, or two tutors arriving at different times with their own delays. Over video, the handover is instant and each child gets a genuine specialist.

Order matters more than people expect. The youngest child should go first, because their session is shortest and their capacity fades fastest, and because a primary slot placed at the end of an evening is the one that gets cancelled when anything else goes wrong. The student with the longest commute goes last, since their arrival sets the lower bound anyway.

It is also worth comparing the children's school calendars once a term. Two schools will have mock weeks a fortnight apart and assessment deadlines that collide with each other's revision. Seeing that in advance lets a family move a slot deliberately rather than cancelling one child's session because the other's crisis arrived first - which, left to itself, always happens to the younger child.

sections.heading: What the school run already costs you
paragraphs: Before any tutoring is purchased, a family in a community like this one spends a significant amount of time on transport. It is worth quantifying, because it reframes what an online lesson is actually saving.

Take a secondary student at a central Sharjah or Dubai school. Forty-five minutes each way, five days a week, is seven and a half hours of weekly travel for the child. If a parent drives rather than using the bus, the parent's time is on top. Over a term that is around ninety hours for the student. None of it is negotiable - school is where it is - but it does explain why a child is tired at five o'clock, and why a plan that assumes an alert student at four is wrong.

Now add an in-home tutor's travel. At market rates an in-home visit is quoted between roughly AED 180 and 500 an hour once the drive is absorbed, against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor teaching online. Over a twelve-week term of weekly sessions, the difference at the middle of each band is several hundred dirhams per subject - money that buys nothing academic. For a household supporting two children, that is a meaningful sum spent on fuel and time.

The honest summary is that living in a quieter community has a transport cost that is already paid in the school run. Adding a tutor's journey on top of it, at a premium, is the avoidable part. These are market figures published so any quote - ours included - can be judged against them; ask us directly for our own, and start with the free trial lesson.

sections.heading: SPEA, the tutor permit and what to ask locally
paragraphs: Two administrative matters are worth settling once, because both become harder to raise later.

The first is the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published - so disregard any amount quoted at you. Because it costs nothing to hold, asking is reasonable and the answer is informative.

The second concerns your child's own teachers. Do not arrange paid tutoring with somebody who teaches and marks your child at school. Abu Dhabi's regulator has published professional-ethics rules barring school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct pointing the same way. The arrangement is convenient and compromises both the marking and the reporting you rely on.

On schools: private education in Sharjah is regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which regulates the emirate's private schools and, with Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge, approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses and assessment methods. Families whose children attend Dubai schools deal with KHDA instead. For our own position, stated plainly: IB Gram holds no approval, licence or accreditation from SPEA, KHDA or any other authority, and has no premises in this country.

sections.heading: Assessed work: the boundary, and why it matters more when evenings are short
paragraphs: Families in commuting communities are under more time pressure than most, and time pressure is what pushes students towards the services that offer to do the work for them. So the boundary deserves stating clearly, in advance.

What a tutor may do is substantial: read the criteria with the student, question a research question until the available data can answer it, teach a technique or statistical method the work requires, review a draft and explain which criterion it fails, and model the same analytical move on different material. What a tutor may not do is write, draft, rewrite or edit any part of the submitted work, or supply a topic with the analysis already completed.

IB Gram does not sell completed internal assessments, extended essays, Theory of Knowledge essays or coursework. Services that do appear in these search results at prices in the thousands of dirhams, and the consequence of using one is a malpractice finding against the student's diploma rather than a problem for the seller. No schedule pressure justifies that risk.

The real protection is structural, and it is the same advice as the rest of this page: plan around the actual available hours rather than the hours you wish you had. A student with a ninety-minute commute has less weekday capacity than their timetable suggests, and a plan that acknowledges it - weekend mornings for assessed work, short weekday sessions for consolidation - does not generate the midnight crisis in which bad decisions get made.

whyPoints.description: We build the slot from your child's real arrival time plus a buffer. Most tutoring arrangements in outlying communities fail on scheduling rather than teaching, and this is the cheapest fix available to a family in Al Rahmaniya.

faqs.question: Can an IB tutor drive out to Al Rahmaniya for lessons?
faqs.answer: Some tutors in the Sharjah market will, and in-home rates are quoted between roughly AED 180 and 500 an hour once travel is absorbed. IB Gram does not: we run no home visits anywhere in the UAE, as that service exists only in India. For a community off Emirates Road the online format solves more than it costs - the session starts when your child is home, runs its full length, cannot be cancelled by traffic, and can be taught by a Diploma specialist who lives anywhere in the country.

faqs.question: What time does a tutoring session realistically start in this community?
faqs.answer: Take your child's actual arrival time and add thirty minutes. For a school in Muwaileh or University City that usually means half past four. For central Sharjah, about a quarter past five. For a Dubai school, six o'clock is often the honest answer. The published school finish time is not a useful input: dismissal, loading, the bus route and afternoon traffic between them can add ninety minutes. One week of noticing when your child walks in gives you the number.

faqs.question: Which schools do most Al Rahmaniya families use?
faqs.answer: Three directions dominate. Muwaileh and University City are closest and produce the earliest arrivals. Central Sharjah - Al Majaz, Al Qasimia, Al Khan - holds a large share of the emirate's places and a slower afternoon journey. And a significant number of families cross into Dubai, which gives the longest commute in the household. Al Rahmaniya itself has very little school provision, so every family here is a commuting family, and the direction they commute in decides their evening.

faqs.question: Why does my child's IB sibling get home so much later?
faqs.answer: Because Diploma provision in Sharjah is concentrated in a small number of schools, so IB families travel further than families on other curricula. The practical effect is that the IB student usually has the longest journey in the house, the lowest weekday capacity, and the greatest need for a punctual slot. Expecting the same evening workload from them as from a younger sibling at a nearer school is the most common planning error we see in households out here.

faqs.question: After a long bus ride, is a Saturday morning slot the better option?
faqs.answer: For work that needs sustained concentration, yes, and noticeably so. Internal assessment planning, a full past paper, an extended essay checkpoint - none of those go well at half past six in a student who left home at dawn. A ninety-minute weekend morning session, when nobody is tired and nothing else is scheduled, is the most underused hour available to commuting families. We would rather move depth there than sell you a third tired evening.

faqs.question: How do we handle three children at three different schools?
faqs.answer: Sequence the evening by arrival time rather than by age or urgency. The earliest arrival goes first, usually the primary child who also needs the shortest session, then the middle child, then whoever has the longest commute. Each gets their own specialist and written plan. Because nobody is driving, handovers are instant and a late bus moves one slot rather than destroying it. A parent then supervises a single evening instead of patrolling four.

faqs.question: What happens to our session when the bus is late?
faqs.answer: It moves by the same amount, usually without anything else changing. That is the main practical difference between an online arrangement and one that depends on somebody's drive: the tutor is not sitting outside a villa or stuck on Emirates Road, so a twenty-minute delay costs twenty minutes rather than the whole lesson. If a day is genuinely lost, we reschedule within the week where the tutor has capacity, and the written plan simply shifts along.

faqs.question: How much time does the school run actually take from a student's week?
faqs.answer: More than most families total up. A secondary student at a central Sharjah school spends around six hours a week in transit; one at a Dubai school, seven to ten. Over a twelve-week term that is seventy-two to one hundred and twenty hours. None of it is negotiable, since school is where it is, but it explains why a child is flat at five o'clock and why a plan assuming an alert student at four does not survive. Build the plan around the energy that is left.

faqs.question: Does the mandatory Arabic and Islamic Education homework affect the plan?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private schools in the UAE must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum, with instructional time counted in forty-minute lesson units, so students arrive home with work from two curricula. In a household where the evening is already shortened by a long commute, that matters: a long general session competes with homework and loses, while a short session on the next dated piece of work survives. We keep sessions to the hour and finish on time.

faqs.question: What does a term of IB tutoring cost for a family out here?
faqs.answer: At market rates rather than ours: a qualified subject tutor teaching online runs roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour across published UAE rate cards, so a weekly slot through a twelve-week term is in the region of AED 1,800 to 3,600 per subject. The in-home equivalent, quoted between AED 180 and 500 an hour with travel absorbed, is several hundred dirhams higher for the same hours - a premium that buys a drive to Al Rahmaniya rather than better teaching. Ask us directly and start with the free trial.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help if my child is too tired to work after the commute?
faqs.answer: Partly, and the rest is scheduling. A good tutor adapts: short problem sets completed inside the session rather than homework set for later, interpretation work rather than extended algebra, and a firm finish time. But if a student is routinely unable to engage at the only weekday hour available, the answer is to move the substantial work to a weekend morning and keep weekdays light. Pretending that a tired hour is a productive one is how families spend a term and see nothing move.

faqs.question: Do tutors in Sharjah need a permit, and should I ask about it?
faqs.answer: Yes, and yes. The private tutor work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Since holding it costs nothing, there is no good reason for a working tutor to be without it.

faqs.question: Our children attend schools in two emirates. Does that complicate anything?
faqs.answer: For tutoring, barely; for school administration, a little. Sharjah's private schools are regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which also approves fees, curricula, programmes, courses and assessment methods, while Dubai's fall under KHDA. So you deal with two sets of published information, two calendars and two sets of internal deadlines. The examination boards, the series and the mark schemes are identical. Comparing both schools' calendars once a term is the practical step that prevents collisions nobody saw coming.

faqs.question: What if no specialist is free at the only hour our commute allows?
faqs.answer: We tell you, and we offer alternatives rather than a substitute. Late slots are in demand precisely because so many families are in this position, so for a narrow course - a higher level language, a less common science - the right specialist may not be free at six on a Tuesday. The options are a different evening, a weekend morning, or a named date when a slot opens. We will not put somebody who has not taught the course into the hour and leave you to discover it.

Lessons for Al Rahmaniya families are one-to-one and online, so nothing waits on Emirates Road.

sharjah/ib-home-tutor-in-al-ramtha.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach IB Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma subjects across Sharjah. Each starts from the most recent evidence - a report, a marked script, a criterion comment - and writes down what the next six sessions will cover, so a parent can judge progress against something specific.

intro.heading: Two moments, one plan
paragraphs: Al Ramtha is an older residential district in the central-western part of Sharjah, with schools in several directions and a long-established tutoring market nearby. Families here rarely struggle to find help. What they struggle with is sequence: knowing what to act on now and what belongs to a later year, which is why tutoring is so often bought in a reaction to a report rather than as part of a plan.

Reports are the usual trigger, and they are a poor instrument for deciding what to buy. A Middle Years report gives criterion levels, which are informative if you read the letters and misleading if you read only the overall grade. A Diploma report gives subject grades on a seven-point scale, often predicted, which compresses several very different problems into one number. In both cases the useful information sits underneath, in a comment or a marked script.

So the first half of this page is a four-week plan for the period immediately after a report: what to ask the school, what to look at, what to test, and only then what to buy. It is deliberately slower than the instinct to book a tutor the same evening, because a fortnight spent identifying the problem makes every subsequent hour more productive.

The second half is organised by year group, because the IB applies pressure in a predictable order. The Middle Years years are deciding habits and, at MYP 5, subject choices. DP1 is deciding understanding, proposals and the shape of the two years. DP2 is deciding whether assessed work is finished before revision begins. A worry that is urgent in one of those years is premature in another, and knowing which is which saves both money and anxiety.

There is also a scheduling constraint worth naming. Diploma provision in Sharjah sits in a small number of schools, so an Al Ramtha student on the programme often travels a fair distance to reach one, and a tutor who also has to drive will offer only a late and unreliable slot. Our lessons are one-to-one over live video, which removes that problem: the session starts when the student is at the desk. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE - home tutoring in a family's house is something we offer only in India.

One more reason to work this way: it protects a family from buying the wrong size of help. The same report can justify three sessions on one topic, a term of weekly work, or a conversation with the school about level - and the difference between those is thousands of dirhams across a Diploma. Identifying which one you need is free, and it is the step that gets skipped.

What follows covers the four-week plan, the year-by-year map, how to read each of the three reports in a school year, the choice points that close options permanently, the final six weeks before any assessment, and what to do with the holidays.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, no external examinations, and the stage where almost nothing is urgent. What is being decided is fluency: reading, number facts, and the habit of writing an answer that addresses the question. Short sessions, aimed at one of those, stopped when the gap closes.

sections.heading: The four weeks after a report arrives
paragraphs: The instinct after a disappointing report is to book a tutor that evening. A better sequence costs a fortnight and makes everything afterwards more effective, because it replaces a grade with a diagnosis.

Week one is for information. Email the relevant teachers and ask three things: which criterion or topic is weakest, what a higher level of achievement would look like on the next task, and whether the subject level or tier is appropriate. Ask for any marked work to come home. For a Diploma student, ask the coordinator for the internal deadline calendar if you do not already have it. None of this costs anything and most families never do it.

Week two is for reading what arrives. In the Middle Years, look at criterion letters rather than the overall grade: a student can be diligent and still score poorly on the criterion asking for evaluation or justified conclusions. In the Diploma, look for the distinction between content not understood, technique not applied, and work not completed on time. Those three have different fixes and different costs.

Week three is for testing. A short diagnostic - a past paper question set, an attempt at higher level material, a draft read against the criteria - converts opinions into evidence. This is the point at which a single paid diagnostic session earns its fee, because a specialist reading a script will see in twenty minutes what a term of general tutoring would eventually reveal.

Week four is for deciding, and only now. With a named weakness, you can buy the right size of help: a three-session repair, a term of weekly work, a change of level discussed with the school, or in some cases nothing at all beyond a change in how the student works. Families who follow this sequence spend less and get more, which is the whole argument for it.

sections.heading: Year by year: what is actually being decided
paragraphs: The IB looks like a continuous ten-year programme and behaves like a series of decision points. Knowing which one your child is at prevents both kinds of error: panicking about something three years away, and discovering too late that a door closed last term.

In the early Middle Years the decisions are about habits, and they are quiet ones. A student who learns to read a command term, structure an investigation and justify a conclusion from the evidence they collected carries that into every later task and into the Diploma. A student who learns to produce neat work on time, without those skills, looks fine on reports and meets difficulty later.

MYP 5 and the pre-DP year are where the big decisions sit: which six subjects, which at higher level, and whether the maths route matches the degree subjects being considered. These decisions are made with less evidence than they deserve, often on the basis of enjoyment and a single set of results. Two or three sessions attempting real higher level material produce better evidence than any amount of discussion.

DP1 is about understanding and proposals: content built properly, an exploration or investigation question settled, an extended essay topic that can actually be answered. DP2 is about completion first and revision second. The table below sets the sequence out so a family can see what belongs to this year and what does not.

Read the final column as seriously as the others. Worrying about internal assessment topics in MYP 4, or about examination technique in DP1, consumes attention that the year's actual job needs - and it is the commonest way a well-meaning household makes a student anxious without making them better.

sections.heading: How to read each of the three reports in a year
paragraphs: Most Sharjah schools issue two or three reports a year, and they are not interchangeable documents. Each arrives at a different point in the teaching and should be read for different things.

The first report of the year is a baseline and little more. In a Diploma subject the teacher may have taught the student for six weeks, and a predicted grade at that stage is a guess with institutional formatting. What is worth reading is the comment: does it describe a student who understands and underperforms, or one who has not yet grasped the material? Those lead to different plans.

The middle report is the most useful one. By then there is real evidence, often including a mock or a substantial criterion-marked task, and the teacher's view has been tested. This is the report to act on, and it is the one that should trigger the four-week sequence described above. It is also the report that arrives when local tutoring availability is about to tighten, which is an argument for acting promptly rather than hastily.

The final report is largely a record. It is too late to change much in the subject it describes, but it is the best evidence available for next year's decisions - subject choices, levels, whether the current approach to independent study works. Families who read it that way get something out of it; families who read it as a verdict do not. For a Middle Years student, it is also the clearest statement of which criteria remain weak going into the following year.

sections.heading: The choice points that close options
paragraphs: Some decisions in the IB are reversible and some are not, and the irreversible ones get less attention than they deserve because they arrive without a deadline attached in the family's mind.

Subject and level choice is the big one. Six subjects, three typically at higher level, chosen at the end of the pre-DP year. Changing a subject early in DP1 is sometimes possible and always disruptive; changing level is easier but has a window. What makes these decisions hard is that the evidence available - last year's grades and the student's preferences - does not predict performance in a specific higher level course very well.

The maths route deserves separate attention. Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation are different subjects, and some university routes in engineering, mathematics and the physical sciences expect the former. A student who chooses the latter because it looks lighter can find a prerequisite missing at application time, by which point nothing can be done. Check the stated requirements of the degree subjects under consideration before the choice is locked, not afterwards.

Then the quieter choice points: whether to take a second language at higher level, whether the extended essay subject suits the student's actual writing strengths, and whether to attempt a subject the school teaches thinly. Each of those is a two-year commitment made in an afternoon. Two or three evidence-gathering sessions beforehand is a small cost against that.
None of this is advice specific to your child, and no page can be. It is a list of the places where a family should slow down and ask for evidence - from the school, and from anybody they are paying.

sections.heading: DP1 and DP2 need different plans
paragraphs: The two Diploma years are often treated as one long run of weekly tutoring. They are different jobs, and a plan that does not change between them wastes the first year and arrives short in the second.

DP1's job is understanding and preparation. Content is being built, and a gap closed now costs one or two sessions where the same gap in DP2 costs five and displaces revision. It is also the year in which the exploration or investigation question is settled, the extended essay subject chosen, and the habit of written method established. The pressure is low, which is exactly why families rarely buy support - and why the ones who do seldom need an emergency later.

DP2's job is completion, then technique. Internal assessments, the extended essay and Theory of Knowledge have to be finished in the first half, because they cannot be done during revision. The final term is timed papers, marked against criteria or mark schemes, with an error log deciding what gets reviewed. A student still writing assessed work in that final term is paying for it twice: once in the marks on that work, and again in the revision time it consumes.

The practical consequence for a family in Al Ramtha watching cost is a shape rather than a quantity: fortnightly in DP1 in the subject that needs it, short fortnightly check-ins on the core components, then a concentrated block in DP2 where the calendar demands it. That typically costs less than weekly support across both years and does more, because every hour has something dated to aim at.

sections.heading: The last six weeks before any assessment
paragraphs: Whatever the year group, the six weeks before a dated assessment have a reliable shape, and most of the value a tutor adds in that window comes from refusing to teach new material.

Weeks six and five are for closing the largest gaps identified by a marked script and for establishing a timed baseline. Weeks four to two are for timed work - full papers or complete criterion tasks - marked between sessions, with an error log kept by question type or criterion. The final fortnight reviews the log and rehearses mechanics: reading the paper, allocating minutes to marks, choosing what to leave until last.

The red flags are equally reliable. New content being introduced in the final fortnight means the plan was wrong. A student who has not completed a full paper under timing by two weeks out is going to meet the clock for the first time in the examination. A tutor who marks generously is producing confidence rather than preparation. And an error log that nobody looks at is a list, not a tool.

For an internal assessment rather than a paper, the same arithmetic applies with different content: the draft should exist three weeks out, feedback should be against the published criteria rather than on prose quality, and the final fortnight should be the student's own revision of their own work. A tutor editing text in the last week has crossed a line that matters more than the deadline does.

sections.heading: What to do with the holidays
paragraphs: The UAE school year has a long summer and several shorter breaks, and they are the cheapest working time available to any family. They are also the time when almost nothing gets done, which is a waste rather than a necessity.

The long summer between DP1 and DP2 is the single most valuable window in the programme. Nothing is due, no tests compete for attention, and three or four sessions can settle an exploration question, plan an investigation's method, do the reading for an extended essay, or clear a content backlog that would otherwise appear during revision. Because lessons are delivered over live video, the slot follows a family who travels, with the timezone adjusted.

Shorter breaks are better used for consolidation than for new work. Two sessions over a mid-year break aimed at the topic that a report flagged will be worth more than four sessions crammed into the following term alongside homework. Ramadan requires its own planning: school days shorten, afternoons are low-energy, and families typically move sessions to after Iftar or to late morning at the weekend. Writing that into the plan before the month starts prevents losing two or three weeks to improvisation.

For a Middle Years student, holidays are the obvious time for criterion work, because the next task has not been set and there is no homework competing. For a pre-DP student, they are the time to attempt real higher level material before a choice is locked. In both cases the work is deliberately finite - a named target and a number of sessions - rather than a holiday-long arrangement nobody wanted.

sections.heading: Deadlines, assessed work and what we will not do
paragraphs: A page about planning should be clear about the boundary that planning protects, because the pressure to cross it always arrives late and never looks like a decision at the time.

A tutor may read the criteria with a student, question a research question until the available data can answer it, teach a method or statistical technique, review a draft and explain which criterion it fails, and model the same analytical move on different material. A tutor may not write, draft, rewrite or edit any part of the submitted work, and may not supply a topic with the thinking already done. IB Gram does not sell completed internal assessments, extended essays, Theory of Knowledge essays or coursework.

Services that do appear in these search results at prices in the thousands of dirhams. The consequence of using one is a malpractice finding against the student's diploma rather than a problem for the seller, and no deadline alters that arithmetic. The defence is the sequence this whole page describes: criteria read early, internal deadlines set before the school's, a draft shown to somebody three weeks out.

Two further limits. We publish no IB examination or results dates, because we could not verify them from the IB's own site - your school's coordinator holds the confirmed version. And we claim no approval, licence or accreditation from SPEA, which regulates private schools in Sharjah and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses and assessment methods, nor from any other authority. IB Gram is a tutor-matching platform with no premises in this country.

faqs.question: Will an IB tutor visit our home in Al Ramtha?
faqs.answer: Some tutors in central Sharjah do, at in-home rates quoted between roughly AED 180 and 500 an hour once travel is absorbed. IB Gram does not: we run no home visits anywhere in the UAE, because that service exists only in India. For an IB family here the online format usually works in your favour - Diploma provision in the emirate is concentrated, so local specialist supply is thin, and video matching reaches a subject teacher wherever they live. The free trial lesson lets you test the format at no cost.

faqs.question: A report just came home and it was bad. What should we do first?
faqs.answer: Not book a tutor the same evening. Spend week one asking the school three questions: which criterion or topic is weakest, what a higher level of achievement would look like on the next task, and whether the level or tier is right. Ask for marked work to come home. Week two, read the criterion letters and comments rather than the overall grade. Week three, test with a diagnostic. Week four, buy the size of help the evidence justifies - which is sometimes a three-session repair rather than a term.

faqs.question: Which of the year's reports should we actually act on?
faqs.answer: The middle one. The first report of the year is a baseline written after a few weeks of teaching, and a predicted grade at that point is a formatted guess - read the comment instead. The middle report has real evidence behind it, often including a mock or a substantial criterion task, and is the one worth triggering a plan. The final report is a record: too late for that subject, and the best evidence available for next year's subject and level decisions.

faqs.question: How do we decide between higher and standard level in a subject?
faqs.answer: By attempting real higher level material and looking at the scripts, not by discussing enjoyment or last year's grade. Two or three sessions on genuine HL questions, marked properly, tell you whether the content is accessible and whether the pace is survivable alongside five other subjects. Also check the stated prerequisites of the degree subjects under consideration, particularly for maths - some engineering and science routes expect Analysis and Approaches, and discovering that at application time is too late.

faqs.question: Does my child's Middle Years report really predict Diploma difficulty?
faqs.answer: The criterion letters do, more than the overall grade does. Middle Years tasks are marked against criteria with task-specific descriptors, and the criteria that ask for evaluation, justification and investigation structure are precisely the skills the Diploma assumes and has no time to teach. A diligent student with weak evaluation scores looks fine on a report and meets trouble in DP1. Those are also the cheapest skills to fix, because there is time and nothing is yet at stake.

faqs.question: Is the maths route decision really that important?
faqs.answer: It is one of the few genuinely hard-to-reverse choices in the programme. Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation are different subjects with different content, and some university routes in engineering, mathematics and the physical sciences expect the former. A student who takes the latter expecting a lighter load may also find the higher level statistics demanding. Check the published requirements of the degrees being considered before the choice is locked, and gather evidence by attempting material from both.

faqs.question: What should tutoring look like in DP1 compared with DP2?
faqs.answer: Different jobs entirely. DP1 is understanding and preparation: content gaps closed cheaply, written method established, the exploration or investigation question settled, an extended essay subject chosen. DP2 is completion then technique: assessed work finished in the first half, timed papers and error logs in the final term. A plan that does not change between the years wastes the first and arrives short in the second, which is the most common pattern we are asked to repair.

faqs.question: How should the last six weeks before an assessment be spent?
faqs.answer: Weeks six and five close the two largest gaps and establish a timed baseline. Weeks four to three are full timed papers or complete criterion tasks, marked between sessions, with an error log by question type. The final fortnight reviews the log and rehearses mechanics - reading the paper, allocating minutes to marks - and introduces nothing new. If new content is being taught in the last two weeks, the plan was wrong, and the honest response is to name what is being abandoned.

faqs.question: Is the summer between the Diploma years worth working through?
faqs.answer: It is the most valuable window in the programme. Nothing is due, nothing competes, and three or four sessions can settle an exploration question, plan an investigation's method, do extended essay reading, or clear a content backlog that would otherwise surface during revision. Families here often travel for part of the break; because lessons are online, the slot follows the student with a timezone adjustment. Students who use it start DP2 level rather than a month behind.

faqs.question: How does Ramadan change the plan for a Sharjah IB student?
faqs.answer: It moves the working hours rather than removing them. School days shorten, afternoons are low in energy, and most families shift sessions to after Iftar or to late morning at the weekend. For a DP2 student with an internal assessment deadline inside the month, rewrite the plan before it begins rather than improvising - improvisation usually costs two or three weeks. Because the lesson is online, moving a slot by two hours requires no renegotiation of anybody's journey.

faqs.question: Why do you not give IB exam or results dates anywhere on this page?
faqs.answer: Because we could not verify them at source: the IB's own site blocks automated access, so no session or results date in this project has been confirmed from the IB itself. A date a parent acts on has to be right, and an FAQ answer is exactly the text that gets quoted back out of context. UAE schools sit the May session, and your school's coordinator holds the confirmed dates for your child's cohort. Cambridge and Pearson dates, which boards publish, we do cite.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with an internal assessment that is close to its deadline?
faqs.answer: With the criteria, the thinking and the feedback - yes. A tutor can narrow a research question so the available data can answer it, teach the statistics or technique the work needs, read a draft and explain which criterion is unmet, and model the same move on other material. A tutor may not write, redraft or edit the submitted text, and IB Gram sells no completed assessments. The malpractice finding attaches to the student's diploma, which is why the deadline does not change the answer.

faqs.question: Does SPEA set the report dates and assessment pattern at our school?
faqs.answer: The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private schools in the emirate and, along with Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge, approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. So your school's assessment pattern and reporting cycle sit inside an approval framework rather than being set freely, and asking for the written calendar is an ordinary request about a document that exists. IB Gram holds no approval or accreditation from SPEA or any other UAE authority and has no premises here.

faqs.question: What if the right specialist is unavailable just after reports go out?
faqs.answer: That is the peak, so it happens. Reports trigger a wave of enquiries across central Sharjah and the specialists in narrow courses are taken first. We will offer a different hour with the right person, or a named date when one frees up, or a single diagnostic session now followed by regular work later. What we will not do is put a generalist into the slot and leave you to discover the mismatch, because for criterion-based work that substitution wastes the term you were trying to save.

intro.heading: The monthly number, not the hourly one
paragraphs: Parents searching for an IB home tutor in Al Suyoh almost always start with an hourly rate and almost always budget in months. Those are different questions and conflating them is how families overspend. An hourly figure of AED 220 sounds manageable until it becomes two subjects a week across a Diploma year, at which point the household is committing to a four-figure monthly line for twenty months. Bestimate's 2026 Dubai estimates put weekly one-hour sessions at roughly AED 240-600 a month at the budget tier, AED 600-1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist exam-year work. Start there and the decisions get sharper.

Al Suyoh is inland Sharjah, a plotted residential district off the Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road corridor with Al Tai and Muwaileh to its north and the Maliha Road running south. It is a car-dependent area where almost every child travels out to school, and that geography has a direct effect on tutoring cost. A tutor willing to drive here is pricing a round trip into the hour. A tutor who does not need to drive here is not. The difference shows up in the monthly total rather than in the headline rate, which is why the headline rate is the wrong place to compare.

IB Gram delivers tutoring to Al Suyoh families as one-to-one lessons over live video, on Gulf Standard Time, scheduled around the Sharjah school day. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; in-home visiting exists only in India, and this page would be useless if it pretended otherwise. What the online format buys is the travel hour back and a tutor pool that is not limited to whoever is prepared to drive out to a plotted suburb on a Tuesday evening.

What follows is the arithmetic a family here would otherwise have to reconstruct from quotes. The market's published monthly packages and hourly bands with their sources. The parts of a quote that are not teaching. The honest cost of an in-home visit expressed as what the premium buys. How many hours a Diploma subject actually absorbs over two years, so you can tell whether a proposed schedule is sensible or merely expensive. And the two checks worth running on any tutor before money changes hands, neither of which costs anything.

One framing is worth stating before the numbers start. Tutoring is one of the few education costs a family controls completely. School fees are set by the school and approved by the emirate's authority; exam entry fees are set by the centre; the timetable is set by somebody else entirely. Tutoring is the line a household can shape to the month, which makes it worth shaping deliberately rather than by reaction. Every figure below is quoted from the source that published it, and none of them is a price of ours. Where this page recommends spending less, it is because less, spent earlier, reliably buys more in this market.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led and transdisciplinary, with no external examinations. Tutoring at this stage is usually about a specific gap, most often reading fluency, number sense or written structure, and it should be short and finite rather than a standing weekly commitment. A PYP family buying a year of weekly sessions is usually buying reassurance rather than progress.
programmes.countryNote: Al Suyoh households with primary-age children often start tutoring because a move between curricula exposed a gap, which is a six-to-ten session problem rather than an ongoing one. The budget question here is straightforward: agree an endpoint before the first lesson, and expect the tutor to tell you when the gap has closed.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Marked against four criteria, A to D, on eight-point scales in each subject group. Costs stay modest through MYP 1 to 3 and rise at MYP 4 and 5, when the Personal Project lands and the written demands start resembling the Diploma's. A report reading 4-5-3-4 is a clearer brief for a tutor than any percentage, because it names which criterion is weak.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Suyoh family planning a Diploma, MYP 4 and 5 is the cheapest place to spend tutoring money, because fixing written structure and command-term discipline here prevents a far more expensive DP1 intervention later. Victoria International School of Sharjah runs the continuum and is the nearest realistic IB route for this part of the emirate.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across HL and SL plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. This is where the monthly figure gets serious, because Internal Assessment deadlines fall while teaching continues and families often add a second and third subject in DP2. The May session is the one UAE schools sit, which fixes when the expensive term falls.
programmes.countryNote: The pattern that wastes money in Al Suyoh is the same every year: nothing in DP1, then three subjects booked simultaneously in the spring of DP2 at exam-term intensity. Spreading one subject across DP1 at a single weekly session costs less in total than the panic version and produces a better outcome, because coursework gets taught rather than rescued.

sharjah/ib-home-tutor-in-al-suyoh.subjectsIntro: Hours needed vary sharply by subject, and so therefore does cost. These notes say what each subject absorbs and where the spend is genuinely worth it for an Al Suyoh Diploma student.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The most expensive subject to leave late. HL carries proof by induction, complex numbers and a deep calculus option, and the method marks go to written justification rather than answers. A student rebuilding reasoning from scratch in DP2 needs roughly twice the hours of one doing it steadily from DP1.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the graphical calculator used, cited and interpreted. Cheaper to support than AA in raw hours, but the exploration eats time if the research question is chosen badly, so the sensible spend is an early block on topic selection rather than a long run later.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and the data-based paper decide grades, and the Internal Assessment is where hours concentrate. Budget a defined coursework block eight weeks before the school deadline; the same work compressed into ten days cannot be taught properly at any price.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics and fields reward drawing before calculating. Paper 2 extended responses pay for stated assumptions. Uncertainty handling in the practical work is a reliable mark leak and takes only two or three sessions to fix, which makes it one of the better-value interventions available.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Volume rather than difficulty. The spend that works is on command terms: outline, explain, distinguish and evaluate each demand a different answer shape, and a student who writes everything they know scores below one who answers the verb. That is technique work, not content delivery, so it is hours-light.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram discipline carries marks prose cannot recover. HL adds calculation and the policy evaluation most candidates leave as assertion. The three commentaries need sourced articles and one clear syllabus concept each, and tutoring them properly is a short block rather than a term.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Individual Oral collapses without two well-chosen extracts and a genuinely arguable global issue, and that is a two-session conversation that saves a grade. Paper 1 unseen commentary improves with marked practice, which means hours spent on feedback rather than teaching.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The HL research project absorbs more time than students expect because it needs real primary material and a tightly bounded question. Content revision is comparatively cheap here; the project is where the hours and therefore the cost sit, and it is predictable enough to budget.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The exhibition and the prescribed-title essay are both method problems rather than knowledge problems. Three or four sessions on how a TOK claim is structured and evidenced is usually the whole intervention, and students who skip it lose points that cost nothing to secure.

subjects.name: Extended Essay supervision support
subjects.description: Not a replacement for the school supervisor. A tutor teaches research-question design, source evaluation and the structure the criteria reward, then reads what the student wrote. Booked as a finite block from topic choice to the first supervisor meeting, it is one of the cheapest points in the Diploma.

sharjah/ib-home-tutor-in-al-suyoh.regionsIntro: Al Suyoh enquiries arrive alongside these neighbouring Sharjah communities. Each has a slightly different cost picture, because school mix and commute distance both move the number.

regions.name: Al Tai
regions.note: Directly north, built around Nasma Residences. Shares schools and school runs with Al Suyoh, so quoted in-home rates here are usually the same, and so is the problem of finding an HL specialist willing to make the trip.

regions.name: Al Rahmaniya
regions.note: Villa community nearby containing Sharjah Sustainable City. Similar plotted layout and similar tutoring supply, which means families in both places compare quotes with each other and find the same narrow in-home pool.

regions.name: Muwaileh
regions.note: Denser, older and school-rich, with Wesgreen International School and the International School of Creative Science inside it. Travelling tutors price Muwaileh lower than Al Suyoh simply because more students sit within one drive.

regions.name: University City
regions.note: Sharjah's higher-education cluster and the source of the market's budget tier, where published rates start around AED 45-65 an hour. Reasonable for lower secondary work, rarely the right purchase for HL sciences.

regions.name: Al Zahia
regions.note: Villa and townhouse community off the E311 with its own retail centre. Diploma families here commute out of the emirate in numbers, which compresses the usable evening and raises what a travelling tutor has to charge.

regions.name: Maliha Road corridor
regions.note: The southern route out of Al Suyoh towards Al Dhaid. Anything beyond it is a long drive for a tutor, which is where in-home quotes stop being competitive and the online option stops having a serious rival.

schoolClusters.city: Al Tai, Muwaileh and University City
schoolClusters.note: The nearest concentration of international-curriculum schools to Al Suyoh, weighted towards British curriculum with IB provision thinner. Fee levels here anchor what families treat as a reasonable tutoring line in the household budget. Students we support attend schools in this cluster.

schoolClusters.city: Sharjah city and Al Hoshi

sharjah/ib-home-tutor-in-al-suyoh.modesIntro: Three formats, three cost shapes. Choosing the wrong one is the most common way an Al Suyoh family spends more than the problem required. All three run online over live video.

modes.title: Single weekly subject, across the term
modes.description: One sixty or ninety-minute session a week in one subject with the same tutor. The lowest sustainable monthly commitment and the format that produces the clearest progress record, because the tutor sees the same student against the same syllabus repeatedly and can say which topics have settled. Most Al Suyoh families should start here and expand only if the evidence says to.
bullets: A fixed weekly slot that can move for a mock week
Written notes after each session naming the next topic
Work drawn from your child's own school scheme of work
Easiest format to stop without wasting a prepaid block

modes.title: Finite coursework block
modes.description: A defined run of four to eight sessions aimed at one piece: an Internal Assessment from research question to a marked draft, a Theory of Knowledge exhibition, or an Extended Essay up to the first supervisor meeting. It has an endpoint, so it has a knowable total cost, which makes it the easiest thing in the Diploma to budget accurately.
